Integrating artificial intelligence into medical device quality systems and health-care practice.
source: PubMed · Expert review of medical devices
desc: [Expert review of medical devices] Quality Control (QC) and Quality Assurance (QA) are central to safety, effectiveness, and regulatory compliance of medical devices. The transition from 21 CFR 820 to the Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR) formalizes harmonization with ISO 13485. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being explored in clinical and manufacturing settings and may support medical-device quality and compliance when appropriately validated. This review examines AI applications within QC, QA, and regulatory systems across the product lifecycle. Health-care examples are included only when they illustrate quality, validation, human oversight, or lifecycle-management considerations relevant to medical devices. Clinical and manufacturing applications are discussed in the context of FDA Computer Software Assurance and quality frameworks. A narrative literature search used PubMed, Google Scholar, FDA.gov, EUR-Lex, and IMDRF.org and covered publications from January 2010 through September 2025. AI can shift medical device QC and QA from reactive approaches toward predictive, risk-based paradigms. When integrated within a robust QMS, AI can improve process capability, reduce human variability, and enable earlier detection of quality and compliance risks. Adoption should be guided by regulatory science, clear intended use, lifecycle validation, effective change control, transparency, and sustained human oversight to protect patient safety and maintain regulatory compliance.

title: Same Question, Different Answers: Auditing Persona-Dependent Variation in Six LLMs on Smoking-Cessation Advice
desc: Hundreds of millions of people now ask large language model (LLM) chatbots for health advice, which raises a question that is simple to pose and hard to answer: does everyone get the same advice? We audit six widely deployed LLMs from four providers on smoking cessation, a domain with codified clini- cal guidance and substantial public-health stakes, by putting the same four cessation questions to twelve user personas that differ in life stage, self-described expertise, and smoking history, for a total of 2,880 responses. What the models say depends on who appears to be asking. Every model named FDA-approved prescription cessation medications less often to teen personas than to adult personas, by 32 to 67 percentage points, and in five of six models a persona presenting health- care expertise received fewer facts than a persona presenting none. We then evaluate one deployable intervention: a short system prompt specifying a factual floor, the set of core med- ical facts every user should receive when they are relevant, while leaving tone, vocabulary, and framing free to adapt. The prompt narrows persona differences in every model, but its effect on overall fact coverage varies in both magnitude and direction across models, so a prompt validated on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another. Two cautions frame these results. Equal mention rates are not always the correct clinical target, because prescription cessation pharmacother- apy is not recommended for minors, so a defensible factual floor must be age-aware rather than uniform. And because our personas vary on several attributes at once, we report scenario- level differences rather than isolated effects of age or expertise. We release all 2,880 responses and the analysis code.

title: J&J MedTech Exec Talks Ottava's FDA Nod and Future
Talking Eyes: Large Language Models for Patient Education in Ophthalmology.
desc: [Ophthalmic epidemiology] The purpose of this study is to investigate the potential of large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT and Google Gemini, to improve health literacy in ophthalmology. By analyzing their ability to provide personalized responses to health-related inquiries, this research aims to assess the effectiveness of these AI tools in addressing ophthalmic conditions. This narrative review analyzed 31 studies evaluating the performance of publicly available LLMs in patient education across various ophthalmic topics. Key parameters assessed included accuracy, accessibility, and adaptability to diverse populations. LLMs produced accurate responses on eye health, simplifying medical information and adapting the readability and language of its outputs. Challenges included occasional misinformation, misunderstood contexts, and Western-centric biases. LLM performance improved when specific strategies were used, such as prompt engineering and revisions of patient education materials by ophthalmologists. LLMs' accessibility harbours the potential to improve ophthalmic health literacy. To maximize their utility, collaborative development with patients and ophthalmologists, legislative oversight, and continuous updates on ophthalmic data are essential.

title: Advancing Clinical Trial Outcome Prediction with Domain-Specific Large Language Models
desc: Clinical trial failures are a major barrier to efficient drug development, incurring substantial costs and delaying patient access to effective therapies. Structured approaches such as the Hierarchical Interaction Network (HINT) predict trial outcomes by explicitly modelling interactions between drugs, diseases and protocols, but make limited use of the free text in trial registrations. We evaluate two domain-specific language models, BioBERT (108M parameters) and BioMistral (7B parameters), for phase-level outcome prediction on the TOP benchmark (12,477 trials), representing each trial as text built from ten ClinicalTrials.gov fields. We compare fine-tuning (full fine-tuning for BioBERT, low-rank adaptation for BioMistral) with probing, in which the pretrained model is frozen and only a lightweight classifier is trained on its embeddings. On the held-out test set of each phase, all four language-model variants achieved higher ROC-AUC (0.613--0.772) and PR-AUC (0.649--0.901) than the published HINT results, corresponding to relative PR-AUC gains of 10--20\%. F1 differences were small and mixed, and no model, including HINT, clearly exceeded the F1 of a trivial classifier that predicts success for every trial. Under the configurations tested, probing performed comparably to fine-tuning: fine-tuned models scored highest on ROC-AUC and PR-AUC in Phases I and II, and frozen BioMistral embeddings in Phase III (ROC-AUC 0.772; PR-AUC 0.901), although most differences between variants were below 0.03 and were not tested for significance. These results suggest that pretrained biomedical representations already encode signal relevant to trial outcome, and that probing is a computationally cheaper alternative to fine-tuning for this task.

title: Resmed CMO on Its Oura and Eight Sleep Partnership Strategy
A scoping review evaluating artificial intelligence applications across various injury prevention domains.
desc: [Injury] Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly utilized for injury prevention across diverse clinical and community settings including machine learning (ML). This scoping review aimed to synthesize the current literature on the applications and predictive performance of AI across multiple injury prevention domains. This scoping review searched five major databases, including PubMed, Embase, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, and the Cochrane Library, to identify studies evaluating AI applications for injury prevention published through May 2026. Eligible studies included original U.S.-based, English-language research across self-harm and suicide, abuse and violence, fall prevention, and sports injury prediction. Studies were excluded if they lacked measurable prevention outcomes or sufficient methodological detail, or focused on injury treatment rather than prevention, to ensure relevant and interpretable evidence for synthesis. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ML models generally outperformed or matched traditional screening methods for self-harm and suicide prediction (AUC 0.81-0.82), while multimodal approaches achieved the highest predictive accuracy (AUC 0.90). In abuse and violence prevention, AI predicted intimate partner violence with an AUC of 0.88 and identified cases before formal disclosure. AI also improved fall risk assessment by accurately categorizing patient risk levels, predicting future falls, and mitigating fall injuries through wearable airbag technology. ML models predicted future sports-related injuries (AUC 0.76-0.84), while identifying modifiable risk factors including workload, strength deficits, prior injury burden, and concussion history. ML-based prediction showed promise for risk stratification in self-harm, suicide, intimate partner violence, and recurrent victimization. Additionally, AI predicted fall risk and identified athletes at risk for future sports-related injuries while detecting modifiable risk factors, including workload, prior injury burden, and strength deficits. Although these findings suggest that AI and ML may have potential applications in supporting earlier risk identification, informing targeted prevention strategies, and facilitating more personalized approaches to injury prevention, the limited available evidence warrants careful interpretation.

title: PsyInterviewee: Informational Invariance and Relational Adaptivity in Mental Health Interview Simulation
desc: LLM-based simulated interviewees support interviewer training and the evaluation of mental health interviewing systems. Existing studies have primarily focused on improving human-likeness through richer patient profiles and behavioral modeling. However, human-likeness alone does not establish their reliability. Reliable simulation requires preserving profile-grounded clinical facts (informational invariance) while adapting disclosure and interaction behavior to the interview (relational adaptivity). To this end, we introduce PsyInterviewee, which separates a protected truth channel from a dynamic interaction channel and verifies generated clinical claims against the profile. Specifically, asymmetric write permissions allow dialogue context to update disclosure and behavioral states without authorizing new clinical facts; these states guide what profile-supported information is revealed and how it is expressed. In an automated evaluation of interactions between LLM-based interviewers and interviewees, PsyInterviewee achieves higher scores than four representative baselines on most metrics across both axes, as assessed by two LLM judges. Ablations suggest that the two channels contribute to clinical grounding and response modulation, respectively.

title: FDA Certified: What It Means and What to Check
Artificial intelligence guided automated image analysis of endobronchial lesions during white-light bronchoscopy to predict moderate to severe airway bleeding.
source: PubMed · Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society
desc: [Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society] Bleeding during flexible bronchoscopy is an important procedural complication, particularly in patients with endobronchial lesions. Early identification of lesions at higher risk may assist bronchoscopists in procedural planning and preparedness. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based image analysis may enable real-time risk stratification during bronchoscopy. In this exploratory observational study, 250 patients with endobronchial lesions undergoing flexible bronchoscopy were analysed. Clinical characteristics, symptoms, bronchoscopic lesion features, and radiological findings were recorded. Procedural bleeding was graded and categorized as nil/mild or moderate/severe. Predictors were identified using Chi-square and multivariate logistic regression analyses. Machine-learning models (Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, CatBoost, and an ensemble classifier) were developed using clinical and bronchoscopic features. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Of 250 patients, 82.8% were male and 60.4% were smokers. Mild, moderate, and severe bleeding occurred in 58.0%, 37.2%, and 3.2% of cases, respectively. Moderate haemoptysis prior to bronchoscopy ( P = 0.028), upper-lobe lesion location on bronchoscopy ( P = 0.013) and computed tomography (CT) ( P = 0.027), and vascular lesion appearance ( P = 0.046) were independently associated with higher bleeding risk. The ensemble model demonstrated the best performance (accuracy 85.0%, AUC 0.88), with higher recall (0.76) compared with individual models. Clinical and bronchoscopic features can help identify lesions at higher risk of bleeding during bronchoscopy. AI-based models showed promising performance and may serve as real-time intra-procedural decision-support tools. Further multicentre studies with external validation are required.

title: Accurate and Auditable ECG Classification via Visibility Graph Neural Networks
desc: Physicians read electrocardiograms (ECGs) from waveform shape and timing, yet accurate deep-learning classifiers rarely show which waveform regions drive their predictions. We introduce LYNX-ECG, a graph neural network that represents each heartbeat as a sparse visibility graph of timestamped turning points. On CODE-Test, LYNX-ECG reaches a macro F1 score of 0.889, outperforming five baselines including the ECGFounder foundation model, while its graphs need about 14% of the storage of graphs built from every sample. Because each node maps to a specific ECG time, we can delete clinically defined waveform regions and alter beat timing to audit predictions. For conduction disorders, the clinically expected region was the strongest evidence in more than 90% of correct predictions. Bradycardia and tachycardia calls follow heart rate with conduction intervals held fixed, and atrial fibrillation calls vanish when beat-to-beat variation is removed. Sparse visibility graphs thus pair accurate ECG classification with clinically grounded, testable explanations.

title: Attitudes of people living with dementia and their carers towards the use of generative artificial intelligence to inform structured medication reviews.
desc: [Age and ageing] Polypharmacy is common in people living with dementia (PLwD) and associated with adverse outcomes. Although Structured Medication Reviews (SMRs) are recommended to optimise medication regimens, their delivery is often constrained by limited resources. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support SMRs, yet little is known about how it is perceived by PLwD and their carers. This study explored their experiences of polypharmacy, views on SMRs and attitudes towards use of AI tools in SMRs. Semi-structured interviews with 12 PLwD experiencing polypharmacy and two focus groups with 14 carers were conducted via Microsoft Teams or telephone and analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Two themes were constructed: participants' perspectives on meaningful SMRs, and embracing AI while preserving patient safety and the human touch. Participants described challenges in managing polypharmacy, with carers playing a central role in supporting adherence and monitoring side effects. Experiences of SMRs varied. SMRs were most valued when clinicians were empathetic and able to offer personalised guidance. Participants viewed AI use in SMRs positively, provided that such tools were well validated and used to assist rather than replace healthcare professionals. AI was also seen as potentially reducing administrative burden and supporting more person-centred care. However, some had concerns regarding patient safety and data security, highlighting the need for appropriate regulation and human oversight. Participants were supportive of AI use in SMRs, despite concerns about safety, data security and disclosure of AI use, and emphasised the importance of patient-clinician interactions and lived experience involvement in AI tool development.

title: VariaFlow: Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
desc: Reconstruction-based anomaly detection no longer fails at reconstruction. Generative models produce high-quality pseudo-healthy reconstructions, and the remaining difficulty is the step of scoring residuals. The residual between a scan and its reconstruction has two indistinguishable sources, genuine pathology and the anatomical variation that separates one healthy brain from another. Scoring against a single reconstruction treats both as anomalous, inflating false positives where healthy anatomy varies most while small or subtle lesions are lost in the surrounding reconstruction error. We identify the missing quantity as the predictive variance, how much a healthy reconstruction can vary at each location. We introduce VariaFlow, which estimates this variance from an ensemble of mask-guided restorations under an unconditional flow matching prior, each started from a different noise initialization, and which normalizes the residual by the resulting standard deviation. Few-step flow matching keeps the ensemble computationally affordable, and restoring at two spatial scales captures lesions of different size. Across three brain MRI datasets spanning stroke and tumor, VariaFlow is trained once on healthy anatomy and generalizes across all three, attaining the highest AUROC (0.94, 0.80, 0.78) on each and the highest AUPRC on both cross-domain datasets, exceeding the strongest baseline by 37% and 50%. Under domain shift, the same baseline drops by up to 52% in AUPRC, whereas VariaFlow stays more stable and achieves the best small-lesion Dice on all three datasets.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Automated Optical Coherence Tomography Analysis for Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Planning: From Plaque Analysis to Precision Lesion Preparation and Stent Optimization.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Heart Association
desc: [Journal of the American Heart Association] Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains the cornerstone of revascularization in coronary artery disease. However, despite advances in stent technology, adverse outcomes related to suboptimal stent placement including under-expansion, malapposition, incomplete coverage, edge dissection, and neoatherosclerosis persist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the highest resolution widely available intravascular imaging modality, allowing unparalleled visualization of stent-vessel interactions and plaque morphology. However, there are significant barriers to large-scale OCT adoption, including time-consuming manual interpretation and dependence on the operator, resulting in significant variability between analysts. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based automated OCT analysis promises to assist PCI by delivering rapid, reproducible, and standardized stent optimization, but current analysis systems lack important features to optimize stent placement. This review summarizes the principles of OCT in PCI, the evidence for OCT-guided optimization, and recent advances in AI-driven automated OCT analysis. We discuss plaque analysis and classification, highlighting how AI-driven automated OCT analysis can identify fibrous, lipid-rich, and calcified lesions and guide tailored lesion preparation using balloons, specialty balloons, drug-coated balloons, intravascular lithotripsy, and atherectomy. We outline emerging AI-enabled workflows for fully automated PCI optimization, evaluate clinical outcomes, interpretability, and workflow integration. Finally, we explore future directions including AI imaging-physiology fusion, multiomics integration, and robotics. If successful, automated AI-empowered OCT analysis could become a central imaging platform for precision PCI, enabling tailored lesion preparation, optimal stent deployment, and improved clinical outcomes in coronary artery disease management.

title: Transferring Peptide-Target Interaction Patterns to Small Molecules by Joint Guidance for Diffusion and Flow Matching
desc: Generating small molecules to target protein-protein interactions (PPIs) remains one of the most challenging yet high-reward frontiers in drug discovery. Unlike traditional small-molecule drugs that bind to deep, well-defined pockets, PPI interfaces often comprise broad, shallow binding surfaces. A natural strategy is to leverage known peptide-target interactions, as peptide ligands provide rich interface-level constraints. However, a major algorithmic challenge is that rigid atom-level conditioning on peptide structures can over-constrain the generative space and exclude valid small-molecule solutions. To address this challenge, we present PIFT (Peptide InterFace Transfer), a novel framework that transfers peptide-target interaction patterns to small molecules through joint sampling-time guidance of masked discrete diffusion and continuous flow matching. PIFT first maps peptide-target and small-molecule-target interfaces into a shared, target-conditioned interaction space, capturing transferable interface information across molecular modalities. The resulting peptide-derived reference then jointly steers building-block logits and 3D coordinates toward peptide-compatible molecules while preserving a strong adapted molecular prior. Extensive experiments across diverse PPI targets show that the learned representation captures cross-modal interaction compatibility, while peptide guidance improves interface recovery and achieves strong docking performance and favorable molecular properties.

title: [Current advances and challenges of artificial intelligence in cervical spine surgery].
source: PubMed · Zhonghua yi xue za zhi
desc: [Zhonghua yi xue za zhi] Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly expanded its applications in medicine, demonstrating potential in imaging analysis, risk prediction, and decision support. Owing to the complexity of disease patterns and the experience-dependent nature of clinical decision-making, AI holds considerable promise in cervical spine surgery. However, most existing studies remain focused on retrospective modeling and technical validation, with limited evidence supporting clinical usability and generalizability. From a clinically driven perspective, this review summarizes the major application scenarios and developmental trends of AI in cervical spine surgery, and highlights key challenges related to causal inference, data quality, multi-center collaboration, and legal and ethical considerations, aiming to provide a rational basis for the standardized application of AI in this field.

title: GazeRIB: Systematic Evaluation of Multi-Reader Gaze-Guided Chest X-ray Learning
desc: Radiologists' visual attention can supervise medical image learning, but how reader panel composition affects its value remains untested. We evaluated GazeRIB (Gaze-guided Radiologist-Informed Blackout), which masks unviewed regions during training and uses unmasked images at inference. Eight experts repeatedly read the same 80 chest X-rays (CXRs). We compared individual readers with three-, five- and eight-reader panels across seven architectures and 10 seeds, evaluating 910 models on a separate 2,897-CXR cohort for four-class severity prediction. Every panel improved macro F1 over the no-gaze baseline by 5.33-7.47 percentage points (pp; Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.007); no individual reader reached significance on this endpoint. Three readers captured 73-80% of the eight-reader gain in macro F1, the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AU-PRC). On external validation without retraining, all four panels improved ROC-AUC on SIIM-FISABIO-RSNA by +1.93 to +4.24 pp (p <= 0.004); on MIMIC-Eye no panel differed significantly from baseline, whereas the single-reader average declined (-1.40 pp, p = 0.008). Reader composition therefore influenced performance, although transfer depended on the cohort.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Supported Patient Navigation Addressing Social Drivers of Health among Vulnerable Adults in Family Medicine and Geriatrics Safety-Net Clinics.
source: PubMed · Journal of health care for the poor and underserved
desc: [Journal of health care for the poor and underserved] Health-related social needs such as housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers are associated with worse health outcomes and increased health care utilization, particularly among older adults. Although health systems increasingly screen for these needs, many lack the capacity to provide follow-up support at scale. This pilot evaluation described the implementation and early operational performance of an artificial intelligence-supported, on-demand patient navigation service integrated into an urban safety-net health system. From July 2024 to March 2025, providers placed 149 referrals from family medicine and geriatrics clinics. Outreach was attempted for all referred patients, and successful contact occurred for 78 patients. Navigators submitted 301 applications for public benefits and community resources; 145 were approved, while others remained pending or in process at analysis. Program costs during the observation period were approximately $5,000. These findings suggest feasibility while highlighting the need for further evaluation of patient experience and outcomes.

title: ReuScope: Auditing Data Reuse and Evaluation Sensitivity in Capsule Vision 2024
desc: We develop ReuScope, a protocol for auditing data reuse and evaluation sensitivity, using Capsule Vision 2024 as a case study. It combines measurements of data relationships with two comparisons: changing the evaluation population while holding predictions fixed, and changing training data while holding evaluation fixed. Byte-identical files cross the public training-validation boundary, and all 41 Kvasir-Capsule recordings that contribute frames occur in both partitions. Shared source recordings establish cross-split overlap; missing cross-recording patient identifiers prevent counting unique shared patients. Across ten paired seeds, removing all training rows attributed to Kvasir-Capsule, plus five rows from other sources flagged as near-matches to it, lowers public-validation balanced accuracy from 82.5% to 61.2%. Evaluating the same fitted models on the validation rows of the other sources reverses the comparison: removal improves balanced accuracy by 1.38 percentage points. The public-validation drop measures sensitivity to source removal, not an amount of leakage-induced inflation. Matched controls show that sample size and class counts alone do not explain the observed score differences. An exploratory experiment removes the training neighbors of validation frames that have close training matches, or equally many distant training rows, and yields a difference-in-differences estimate, relative to matched unflagged frames, of -0.355 percentage points in true-class probability; the paired-t interval for accuracy spans zero. The resulting procedure distinguishes observed reuse from conditional performance sensitivity and specifies the population, class support and uncertainty unit for each conclusion.

title: How should junior doctors navigate artificial intelligence clinical advice?
desc: [Internal medicine journal] Artificial intelligence (AI) clinical decision support tools are becoming increasingly integrated into medical decision-making, offering rapid, evidence-based clinical recommendations. While surrounding discussion has largely focussed on senior clinicians, junior doctors, responsible for many day-to-day decisions in hospitals, face unique challenges in navigating these technologies among the many existing information sources. This paper examines the epistemic, ethical and practical implications of AI use by junior doctors, highlighting its potential to streamline knowledge access, as well as risks including automation, bias and deskilling. We introduce a suggested framework to help junior doctors navigate AI clinical advice and integrate it safely into clinical practice, among other information sources.

title: Measuring What Matters: A Causal Reliance Score for Histopathology Image Segmentation
desc: Reliable histopathology segmentation requires models that rely on pathology-relevant structures rather than spurious background correlations. In this work, we argue that improving architectures alone is insufficient if models continue to rely on spurious correlations rather than pathology-relevant features. We introduce a causality-inspired evaluation framework based on controlled interventions that explicitly probes model sensitivity to foreground tissue structure and background/domain variation. Building on this, we propose the Causal Reliance Score (CRS), a metric that quantifies the relative sensitivity of model predictions to foreground perturbation versus background/domain variation under controlled interventions. To support this analysis, we design augmentation strategies that act as implicit counterfactual interventions during training, encouraging invariance to nuisance factors while preserving morphology. We demonstrate how these interventions reveal behavioural differences between models that are not captured by standard metrics such as Dice or IoU. While we instantiate our framework using a self-supervised transformer (CAUSE-ViT), the primary contribution of this work is not a new architecture, but a principled intervention-based methodology and evaluation metric for auditing model behaviour in medical image segmentation. Our results suggest that evaluating model behaviour through counterfactual interventions is essential for developing reliable and clinically robust medical image segmentation systems.

title: Clot waveform analysis in haemostatic and systemic disorders: current applications and clinical potential.
source: PubMed · Journal of thrombosis and thrombolysis
desc: [Journal of thrombosis and thrombolysis] Clot waveform analysis (CWA), originate from conventional coagulation assays, particularly the activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) and prothrombin time (PT), offers enhanced sensitivity and dynamic profiling of haemostatic processes. By capturing real-time changes in clot formation kinetics, CWA patterns provide disease specific changes beyond traditional clotting time. It has potential clinical utility in identifying bleeding risk in inherited and acquired bleeding disorders, as well as prothrombotic states in condition such as infections and myocardial infarction. A unique APTT second-derivative curves have been reported in COVID-19 infection. In malignancy, it may help clinicians to mitigate the risk of developing thrombotic complications due to cancer-associated hypercoagulability. This review covers the principles, analytical parameters, and clinical applications of CWA. As evidence continues to grow, integrating CWA into standard coagulation testing algorithms, particularly with the use of artificial intelligence, may potentially lead to improvements in patient stratification, monitoring and management in both acute and chronic haemostatic disorders.

title: Enhancing Medical Lesion Segmentation via Several Simple Modules
desc: This work introduces three lightweight enhancement modules for medical lesion segmentation to improve clinical applicability, particularly under data-scarce and computationally constrained environments. Current mainstream methods struggle with the lack of high-quality annotations for rare pathologies, which often leads to severe morphological distortions during inference, despite achieving seemingly ideal DSC scores. Furthermore, the isolated development of individual segmentation tasks restricts cross-domain methodological innovation, underscoring the need for leveraging shared knowledge across different lesions within the same anatomical region. However, constrained access to historical data and annotations hinders efficient knowledge extraction and triggers catastrophic forgetting when adapting to new classes. To address these challenges, we first propose DT-Morph Combined Loss with continuous spatial pooling to optimize differentiable topological structures and boundary continuity. Second, we introduce 3D Group Prompt, which extracts domain-universal knowledge via curated volumetric image-mask alignment prompts together with text prompts built on SAT baseline. Finally, we replace conventional output layers with Many-to-One Conditional Segmentation Head equipped with synonym-resolved routing, which brings negligible computational cost and enables fast incremental learning for new categories without sacrificing performance on old tasks. Ablation studies on abdominal and extra-abdominal datasets covering both organ and lesion segmentation verify the efficacy of our modules.

title: AI Literacy as a Leadership Competency: Preparing Nurse Executives for Artificial Intelligence Governance.
source: PubMed · The Journal of nursing administration
desc: [The Journal of nursing administration] Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly integrating into health care delivery, influencing clinical, operational, and strategic decision-making. Nurse executives must therefore possess competencies that enable informed oversight of AI-enabled systems. This article proposes an AI literacy competency framework for nurse executive practice, adapted from existing AI literacy scholarship and aligned with nursing leadership responsibilities. The framework provides a conceptual foundation for integrating AI literacy into leadership competency development, translating theoretical constructs into practice that is aligned with executive decision-making. The framework also defines knowledge, skills, and attitudes necessary for ethical governance, evaluation, and responsible implementation of AI in health care organizations. In doing so, it offers a structured approach for preparing nurse leaders to guide the responsible adoption and oversight of AI-enabled technologies.

title: A Unified XAI-NSAI Analytical Framework for Trustworthy IoT Anomaly Detection
desc: The widespread deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in critical environments makes anomaly detection essential for identifying abnormal behaviors and supporting timely investigation and response. However, accurate detection alone is insufficient. Practical IoT deployments must also provide explanations, incorporate domain knowledge and reasoning, operate under IoT constraints, and support human decision making. Although recently proposed approaches increasingly incorporate Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) or Neuro-Symbolic Artificial Intelligence (NSAI), XAI and NSAI methods are often considered independently. We argue that they should be considered together to better understand their complementary roles in supporting trustworthy IoT anomaly detection. To address this gap, we propose a unified analytical framework organized around five complementary dimensions. The framework provides a structured basis for characterizing existing approaches, identifying capability gaps and design trade-offs, and guiding the design of new anomaly detection systems for different IoT applications. We demonstrate the framework's analytical utility by applying it to three representative studies and illustrate its design utility through its application to a Medical IoT anomaly detection system.

title: Emergency medicine literature in the Web of Science category "emergency medicine": A bibliometric analysis (1980-2024).
source: PubMed · Turkish journal of emergency medicine
desc: [Turkish journal of emergency medicine] The objective is to describe long-term trends in emergency medicine (EM) research output from 1980 to 2024 and to map study designs, conceptual domains, and collaboration structures within the Web of Science (WoS) Category "EM." We conducted a retrospective bibliometric analysis of records indexed in the WoS Core Collection from January 1, 1980, to December 31, 2024, using the WoS Categories filter "EM." The search was performed on October 3, 2025. Only records with WoS document type "Article" were included. Bibliographic data, including publication year, journal, country, institutions, citations, and indexed keywords/metadata, were extracted. A rule-based text-mining algorithm classified study designs and conceptual domains and was internally validated against a manually reviewed sample of 240 records, showing 75.8% agreement (κ = 0.638) for study design and 86.3% agreement (κ = 0.828) for conceptual domain. Descriptive statistics and VOSviewer-based co-authorship, co-citation, and keyword co-occurrence analyses were performed. Of 161,842 records initially identified, 102,561 articles met eligibility criteria. Annual EM publication counts increased after 2000. Health services and systems research and observational clinical studies predominated, whereas randomized controlled trials and qualitative or mixed-methods studies remained uncommon. Trauma, resuscitation, cardiovascular emergencies, and sepsis were longstanding core domains, while digital health, artificial intelligence, point-of-care ultrasound, disaster medicine, and global EM gained prominence after 2010. Collaboration expanded over time, but multinational co-authorship remained limited, and affiliations from low- and middle-income countries were underrepresented. EM has evolved into a high-volume, thematically diverse field, but its evidence base remains predominantly observational and geographically imbalanced.

title: RECITE: Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence
desc: Overly restrictive eligibility criteria contribute to widespread enrollment failure in clinical trials, yet published recommendations for how specific criteria should be broadened remain disconnected from trial design at scale. We introduce RECITE (Revising Eligibility Criteria Incorporating Textual Evidence), a framework for automated discovery, extraction, and implementation of evidence-based eligibility criteria revisions. RECITE uses protocol amendment documents from ClinicalTrials.gov to construct a dataset of 11,913 curated instances across 5,735 trials, each pairing original criteria with documentary evidence and target revisions. We benchmark fifteen LLM configurations under truncated-to-context-window and retrieval-augmented generation conditions, on a 3,116-instance sample under an LLM-as-judge protocol validated against ten domain experts (judge vs. human quadratic-weighted Cohen's $κ_{qw} = 0.694 \pm 0.096$). The best open-weight model, Gemma 2 9B, achieves $κ_{qw}$-aligned ordinal score $3.0 \pm 0.9$ on a 0--4 scale (normalized 0.742) and the best closed-weight model, GPT-4o, reaches $3.0 \pm 0.8$ (normalized 0.745). Using an agentic literature discovery system, we then identified 44 paper--trial matches across five publications providing trial-design and EC-modification evidence. Our findings suggest that existing clinical knowledge can be operationalized into actionable trial design recommendations.

title: Chemistry-transforming applications of artificial intelligence.
desc: [Chemical Society reviews] Artificial intelligence is increasingly used across chemical research, but its practical value depends on where it intervenes in the workflow and how reliably it generalizes beyond curated benchmarks. This review adopts a pipeline-based perspective: we first decompose chemical research into stages that generate, transform, and validate information and then map AI methods onto these stages with an emphasis on measurable outcomes and failure modes. We summarize classical machine learning and emerging chemistry-informed and foundation model approaches, highlighting recurrent pitfalls such as data leakage, overfitting, and extrapolation. We then critically survey applications spanning knowledge extraction, experimental data interpretation (including data from spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, and microscopy), property and reactivity prediction, synthesis planning, and closed-loop experimentation, focusing on representative case studies that illustrate transferable design patterns rather than exhaustive coverage. Across these domains, the evidence supports a shift from static structure-property thinking toward dynamic, data-rich decision cycles where models prioritize experiments, extract mechanistic descriptors from complex signals, and guide iterative refinement under constraints. We conclude by outlining requirements for robust deployment and discussing near-term directions for chemistry-grounded foundation models and intelligent experimental platforms.

title: With foundation-model features, aggregator complexity does not improve cross-hospital discrimination in gastric whole-slide image classification
desc: Whole-slide image classifiers are usually developed within one hospital and often go untested at unseen hospitals. We assembled 5,036 haematoxylin-and-eosin-stained gastric slides from five Korean hospitals, scanned at 20x and 40x, and compared multiple-instance learning aggregators under leave-one-hospital-out validation on frozen pathology foundation-model features. A hierarchical patch-region-slide graph aggregator (CHIME-MIL) with site alignment and two-scale fusion reached a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.837, above six conventional attention and transformer aggregators trained without these steps. Under a matched recipe it did not exceed attention-based pooling, and global max pooling given the same alignment and fusion was better (AUC 0.855, P = 0.0002). The alignment, which subtracts each hospital's mean feature vector without labels, onboarded a new hospital from ten unlabelled slides and cost 0.002 AUC without held-out-hospital data, but its accuracy gains were small and inconsistent. The model had low top-label calibration error (0.053) but under-confident malignancy probabilities, and removing its most-attended patches lowered the malignancy probability far more than removing random patches. With these features, more complex aggregators did not improve discrimination; what a deployable system adds is label-free onboarding, calibration checks and auditable evidence.

title: Designing Care into the System: Age, Universal Design, and the Limits of AI Empathy.
source: PubMed · Studies in health technology and informatics
desc: [Studies in health technology and informatics] Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in contexts that serve older adults, yet they are frequently evaluated on the basis of linguistic fluency rather than structural inclusion. This paper argues that current large language model based AI systems fail a fundamental Universal Design test when applied to ageing populations. Two structural failures are identified: the systematic underrepresentation of older adults in training data, and interaction design assumptions calibrated to digitally fluent younger users. These failures produce simulated empathy, a form of linguistically competent but structurally misaligned responsiveness. Drawing on the Timeless pilot, a voice-first AI lifestyle ecosystem designed for older adults, the paper demonstrates how Universal Design principles can be embedded at the level of AI infrastructure through affordance recalibration, pacing modulation, and cross-domain consolidation. A three-part evaluative framework is proposed, centred on representational inclusion, affordance inclusion, and institutional inclusion, to assess AI systems against Universal Design standards. The framework positions AI accessibility as a structural design imperative rather than a post-hoc remediation.

title: Different Models, Shared Failures: Auditing Frozen-Encoder Pools for Medical Segmentation
desc: Average segmentation accuracy and model count do not reveal whether models fail on the same cases. We present CoFailMed, an audit of correlated failures in pretrained-encoder pools for medical segmentation. Across five 2D tasks, we evaluate 11 public pretrained encoders (a controlled sample, not a census) using frozen features and separately trained $1\times 1$ readouts with four seeds per encoder. Shared-checkpoint pairs have the highest mean per-case Dice correlation. An expanded 17-encoder analysis shows that distinct checkpoints within the same encoder family remain more correlated than cross-family pairs. At the pooled 33rd-percentile Dice threshold, four-member pools drawn from distinct encoders have mean effective sizes of 1.56-2.92, estimated from failure correlations in pools with enough failures and passes per member. In the primary pool, richer readouts and fine-tuning narrow the Dice-correlation gap between pairs sharing a checkpoint (or the DINOv2-B/S release) and all other pairs. Yet dependence between different encoders can increase, and fine-tuning does not consistently increase effective pool size at 33rd-percentile thresholds recomputed for each training recipe. A smaller between-group gap can coexist with greater dependence. Pool evaluation should therefore report absolute dependence and threshold-specific effective size alongside accuracy and nominal pool size. The CoFailMed release provides aligned per-case traces, analysis scripts and study code to reproduce the central audit results.

title: CSF cytology: core principles, diagnostic pitfalls and emerging digital tools including artificial intelligence and telecytology.
desc: [Acta neuropathologica] Cerebrospinal fluid cytology remains a cornerstone of diagnostic evaluation in infectious, autoimmune, haemorrhagic, and neoplastic disorders of the central nervous system despite advances in neuroimaging, molecular diagnostics, and digital technologies. This narrative review summarises established principles of cerebrospinal fluid cytology, highlights methodological limitations and diagnostic pitfalls, and integrates emerging developments, including automated cell counting, artificial intelligence, and telecytology. Pre-analytical factors are critical determinants of diagnostic accuracy. Delayed sample processing promotes pH-dependent autolysis and substantial cell loss, whereas rapid cytocentrifugation preserves cellular morphology and facilitates reliable assessment. Automated cell counters are increasingly implemented in routine laboratories and offer advantages in settings with limited technical staffing. However, current systems show limited precision in samples with low and slightly elevated cell counts and limited morphological evaluation. Manual chamber counting, particularly in the normal and low-cell-count range, remains the gold standard for quantitative CSF cell assessment, whereas expert microscopic examination remains the reference standard for qualitative cytomorphological assessment. Although the sensitivity of neuroimaging continues to improve, cerebrospinal fluid cytology retains a unique diagnostic role in the detection of infectious and neoplastic conditions and in the evaluation of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Cytological detection of erythrophages, siderophages, and haematoidin crystals can reveal haemorrhage and provide clues to its temporal stage. Overall, cerebrospinal fluid cytology remains a valuable diagnostic tool when integrated with clinical, laboratory, microbiological, immunological, and imaging findings. Careful recognition of common pitfalls is essential. We recommend rapid cerebrospinal fluid processing, routine preparation of cytospin-based stained slides with expert microscopic review, and the implementation of automated or digital methods only within clearly validated workflows.

title: AI algorithms and external validation: promises, pitfalls, and a practical blueprint.
desc: [European heart journal] External validation involving the testing of a frozen AI model on independent data from other sites, populations, time periods, or devices provides the clearest estimate of intended-use setting performance when those external data are deployment-representative of the expected population, measurement processes, and clinical workflow. It yields realistic estimates of discrimination and calibration, exposes shortcut learning and distribution shift, quantifies clinical utility through decision-analytic measures, and reveals subgroup disparities requiring mitigation. Yet common pitfalls undermine credibility: quasi-external splits with hidden relatedness; spectrum and prevalence mismatch; site, workflow, and hardware effects; label noise and reference-standard drift; analytic flexibility and selective reporting; small, underpowered samples; reliance only on the area under the curve; unreported threshold tuning; and leakage. A practical blueprint emphasizes pre-registration; representative, multi-site cohorts spanning geography, time, and acquisition; prevention of patient and temporal overlap; comprehensive evaluation of discrimination, calibration (including calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and calibration plots), and net benefit with confidence intervals; pre-specified subgroup and fairness audits; transparent labelling procedures and uncertainty analyses; principled sample-size calculations; and minimal, well-documented model updating (recalibration before revision). Finally, external validation should connect to post-deployment governance via drift detection, performance triggers, and change-control plans, complemented by site-specific local evaluation to ensure safety and reliability across diverse clinical environments. When executed to these standards, external validation transforms promising prototypes into dependable clinical tools, clarifying where a model performs, where it fails, and what adaptations are necessary for safe, equitable, and sustainable use. This framework links statistical evaluation to clinical use, model updating, and post-deployment monitoring.

title: Global Virology Meets the Viruses of the Changing World: Where Ecology, Evolution, One Health, Artificial Intelligence, and Innovation Unite to Decode Viruses.
desc: [Virusdisease] This article highlights the current issue of VirusDisease in the fast-changing scenario of modern virology and introduces the VIROCON 2026, the flagship national conference of the Indian Virological Society, which will be held in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, on 11-13 November 2026 with the theme "Viruses in the ChangingWorld: Ecology, Evolution and Future Preparedness." The current issue covers the wide range of contemporary virological research, including molecular and structural virology, emerging and re-emerging viruses, diagnostics, computational methods, epidemiology, co-infections, and viral evolution. VIROCON 2026 builds on this interdisciplinary perspective with eight thematic tracks that combine One Health, AI, metagenomics, ecology, climate change, therapeutics, vaccines, and preparedness. The issue and conference highlight the need for collaboration, innovation, and globally connected virology to prepare for and address future viral threats.

title: Promoter Prediction in Helicobacter pylori Strain 26695 by Using a Deep Neural Network.
source: PubMed · Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)
desc: [Methods in molecular biology (Clifton, N.J.)] To initiate gene transcription, RNA polymerase binds to the upstream genomic region of the gene called the promoter. As the most important component of the genome, gene expression is regulated by promoter identification. The present work employed a deep learning technique to predict promoter sequences in Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) strain 26695. Here, we used evolutionary scale modeling (ESM) and one-hot encoding to encode the promoter sequence, and then these encoded features were given as an input to the convolutional neural network (CNN) based classifier by utilizing tenfold cross-validation (CV). The results of the anticipated model showed reasonable performance, with an accuracy of 88.71%.

title: AxialTAD: an axial contrast architecture for TAD boundary prediction from Hi-C.
desc: [Briefings in bioinformatics] Topologically associating domains (TADs) are fundamental units of 3D chromatin organization, and accurate identification of TAD boundaries from Hi-C contact matrices remains an active challenge. Recent deep learning approaches have advanced substantially, but these rely on increasingly large architectures, raising the question of how much of this capacity boundary-centric analysis requires. Here we propose AxialTAD, a compact deep learning model centered on an Axial Contrast Module (ACM) that explicitly encodes directional contrast in contact intensity along the row and column axes of local Hi-C patches, an operator aligned with the geometric signature of TAD boundaries. Evaluated on four human cell lines (GM12878, HeLa-S3, IMR-90, K562) within cell lines and under leave-one-cell-out generalization, AxialTAD performed comparably with a recent convolutional neural network (CNN)+Transformer baseline (deepTAD) while using 76%-80% fewer trainable parameters (113K-137K versus 571K). A parameter-matched conventional CNN achieved similar F1 to AxialTAD in the human 25 kb experiments. When trained and evaluated within each of two mouse datasets, AxialTAD outperformed both this control and deepTAD. Orthogonal validation against CTCF and cohesin ChIP-seq supported the biological plausibility of the predicted boundaries. These results indicate that, within the range of architectures examined, a large architecture is not necessary to reach this level of boundary prediction.

title: Colorimetric sensor arrays and artificial intelligence for natural product quality evaluation: From cross-reactive fingerprints to analytical validation.
desc: [Talanta] Natural products encompass traditional Chinese medicines, herbal medicines, teas, food-derived plant materials, plant extracts, and naturally occurring bioactive compounds. Their rapid identification and quality evaluation require a balance among integrative characterization, analytical accuracy, and field accessibility. Empirical authentication methods are difficult to quantify and reproduce, whereas confirmatory techniques based on chromatography, mass spectrometry, and spectroscopy, although analytically reliable, cannot fully meet the frequent demands of on-site screening, process monitoring, and risk triage. A colorimetric sensor array (CSA) generates sample-specific color fingerprints through cross-reactive responses across multiple sensing elements. Combined with standardized image acquisition, feature extraction, and chemometric or machine-learning analysis, CSA-based workflows can support classification, quantitative prediction, and anomaly detection. This integrated strategy is referred to here as CSA-AI, an umbrella term that does not equate conventional chemometrics with artificial intelligence (AI). This review critically examines CSA design, color-data acquisition, chemometric and AI-assisted analysis, analytical validation, and applications in natural product quality evaluation along the chain of "array response-color fingerprint-computational interpretation-quality decision-making." Particular attention is given to authentic complex matrices, sample-level data partitioning, data leakage, independently sourced external evaluation, cross-device transfer, validation evidence, model interpretability, and confirmation by established analytical methods. Current direct visible-CSA evidence is strongest for authentication and preliminary adulteration screening, whereas process monitoring, storage-deterioration warning, and field deployment remain less thoroughly validated. Current evidence supports CSA-AI primarily as a complementary tool for rapid screening, risk warning, and auxiliary grading rather than as a replacement for confirmatory methods such as HPLC, GC-MS, and LC-MS.

title: Unit-Area Optimized Flexible Triboelectric Nanogenerators for High-Performance Human Motion Sensing With Deep Learning.
source: PubMed · Small (Weinheim an der Bergstrasse, Germany)
desc: [Small (Weinheim an der Bergstrasse, Germany)] Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) have garnered significant attention as self-powered energy harvesters and sensors, yet their performance critically depends on structural design and material engineering. In this work, we introduce a structured TENG designed with the concept of unit-area to maximize contact efficiency by minimizing mechanical interference between neighboring structures. Synergistically, barium titanate (BaTiO3) nanoparticles were incorporated into the elastomer matrix to enhance the dielectric constant and surface charge density. Based on this approach, unit-area-based TENGs (UA-TENGs) with various geometries were comprehensively evaluated through computational analysis and experimental validation. The results reveal that smaller structures enable more effective contact, while dome structures exhibit superior output compared to pyramid structures. Quantitatively, the optimized dome-structured UA-TENG with the BaTiO3 composite achieves a power density of 18 W/m2, a maximum voltage of 254 V, and enhanced pressure sensitivities. The device successfully powered 127 LEDs and operated small electronics. Furthermore, the UA-TENG demonstrated excellent performance in detecting biomechanical signals. Integration into a smart glove enabled real-time gesture recognition, where a convolutional neural network accurately classified five distinct hand motions to achieve reliable wireless drone control. These results demonstrate the broad application prospects of the UA-TENG in wearable energy supply, intelligent sensing, and human-machine interaction.

title: An evaluation framework for sparse 4D (3D + time) imaging reconstruction via bootstrapped cross-validation.
desc: [Journal of microscopy] Four-dimensional (4D; 3D + time) microscopic imaging has emerged as a powerful technique for investigating dynamic phenomena in complex systems, enabling direct visualisation of structural evolution in space and time. However, when pushing the limits of spatiotemporal resolution, most time-resolved imaging techniques yield inherently sparse 4D datasets. While deep learning-based reconstruction methods have shown promise in reconstructing 4D from sparse spatiotemporal measurements, a practical approach for evaluating their performance in the absence of a 4D reference has, to the best of our knowledge, been lacking. Here, we present a bootstrapped cross-validation framework that estimates reconstruction performance by quantifying correlations between reconstructions generated from independently sampled subsets of the acquired data, as inspired by the 3D validation strategy in cryo-electron microscopy, where reconstructions from split datasets are compared to assess resolutions. This enables both qualitative and quantitative assessment in the absence of ground truth. We investigate two representative scenarios with sparse and ultra-sparse X-ray datasets and validate this approach using 4D-ONIX, a 4D deep-learning reconstruction method, on simulated water droplet collision experiments. The proposed approach provides a reference-free framework for performance estimation and support for better-informed experimental strategies across a wide range of ultrafast imaging applications.

title: Institutional digitalization and digital stress: a four-wave observational study of teacher-reported AI-collaborative teaching in physical education.
desc: [Frontiers in psychology] How institutional digitalization relates to teachers' experience of work and subsequent artificial intelligence (AI)-supported practice remains unclear. Drawing on job demands-resources principles, we examined these relationships in a four-wave observational cohort of 961 physical education teachers from 120 Chinese institutions. We linked an organizational-source digitalization proxy to teacher questionnaires and a study-specific teacher-reported score of AI involvement in teaching tasks. Analyses adjusted for baseline practice and separated between-institution from teacher-relative associations. Two of five primary tests met the Holm-adjusted criterion. The stress-related product of between-institution coefficients was negative (-0.099; pointwise 95% confidence interval [-0.184, -0.033]). The positive digitalization-stress association was weaker among teachers with higher digital self-efficacy relative to colleagues (interaction coefficient -0.101; [-0.168, -0.037]) but remained positive at the low, average, and high self-efficacy levels examined. The adjusted digitalization-practice association, appraisal-related coefficient product, and appraisal interaction did not meet the corrected criterion. The findings connect the organization and experience of work with reported AI practice, emphasizing perceived digital work pressure and relative self-efficacy while complementing accounts centered on technology acceptance.

title: Sequence Scanning Improves Accuracy for Antibody-Antigen and Molecular Glue Ternary Complex Cofolding.
desc: [ChemMedChem] Accurately modeling biomolecular interactions is crucial for understanding biological function and can accelerate drug discovery efforts. Deep-learning-based cofolding methods such as AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2 can successfully predict many different biomolecular complexes. However, these models show lower success rates in predicting antibody-antigen and molecular glue (MG) ternary complexes, two cases of high relevance to pharmaceutical research. Here, we present sequence scanning, a new workflow, evaluated on Boltz and Protenix, that improves prediction accuracy in these domains by applying systematic constraints to enhance overall sampling diversity. For both use cases, we assess the performance of the method on large, diverse benchmark sets. We find improved accuracy of the sequence scanning workflow in predicting antibody-antigen interface contacts and in pose prediction quality for MGs compared to previously published results. We also discuss remaining challenges and potential improvements to the method.
